rv.q: These plays are packed with nifty zingers and have been directed by John Turturro with a boisterous flair for socking home the borscht-belt humor.
Squeezing three playwrights into a single show is dangerous business, particularly when they're all tacking the reality of relatives, but only Allen seems to have emerged the stronger for the effort.
Unfortunately, throwbacks, if they are to get somewhere, need to have aim, momentum and a sense of direction.
Although Allen has dragged the corny borscht-belt routines out of the trunk in affectionate homage, bad jokes are still bad jokes.
But Talking Cure is the least satisfying item on a stale menu.
You may also wonder why theatergoers aren't rioting for a refund.
The theory is impeccable, the results disastrous.
Relatively Speaking is, comparatively speaking, far from any of its creators' finest work.
While its premise may particularly appeal to men of a certain age who fancy women half their age, the laughter was co-ed.
However, the preceding two pieces provide mixed results.
For these accounts of homegrown neuroses — by veteran wits Elaine May, Ethan Coen and Woody Allen— offer both disarming highs and disappointing lows.

But given the estimable writers of the pieces, Ethan Coen, Elaine May and Woody Allen, and the proven talents of the high-profile ensemble, it’s difficult to not be disappointed by the production, which should be the comic pinnacle for the Broadway season.
Unfortunately, “George is Dead,” the second one-act of the evening takes a thin and obvious premise, exacerbating the character’s motives until it becomes anxiety provoking to sit through.
This is just an old-fashioned, third-rate farce and is hardly worthy of being done on Broadway.
Relatively speaking, Relatively Speaking is a bust.
Credit both Thomas and Lisa Emery for giving it their best shot but what really dies here is the comedy.
That this level of writing talent could produce such a lethargic, laugh-free evening is a mystery and a tremendous disappointment.
It’s all very loud, very fast and remarkably pointless.

cn.t: This trio of one-acts from Woody Allen, Elaine May, and Ethan Coen disappoints despite the star-studded writing lineup, delivering mixed-to-negative results with only sporadic laughs and flat direction by John Turturro.

sg.ra: Lena Horne is one of the smaller Nederlander houses (1,069 seats) and the front orchestra AAA/AA rows sit unusually close to the stage with an unraked front section — TripAdvisor reviewer in Row C reported head-blockage from the flat rake, so row B center is the sweet spot for SIX-style concert staging.

Mezzanine overhang at Lena Horne starts at Row J (Headout/TickPick), so rows E-I stay fully open to the ceiling — critical here because the house has only 18 orchestra rows (AAA-Q) and the overhang drops in early relative to larger Nederlander houses.

Headout and TickPick both pin mezzanine overhang start at Row J — with only 18 orchestra rows total, roughly the back half of the Lena Horne orchestra sits under that overhang and loses upper-stage visibility; NYTix specifically flags the side orchestra seats as 'aren't very comfortable'.

Lena Horne's front mezz is unusually shallow — only 4 rows (A-D) per BroadwayDirect chart — so even Row D sits close to the stage with 'advantageous' sightlines (Headout), and the bar is on the mezzanine level (NYTix) making this the most practical tier in this Nederlander house.

Because the front mezz only has 4 rows at Lena Horne, 'rear' of front mezz (C-D) is still just 3-4 rows from the rail — AVFMS R-D-16 and R-C-26 both reported clear views, and these are priced as value seats while Row A commands premium.

Rear mezz at Lena Horne is 8 rows (E-M) continuous with the front mezz balcony — there's no secondary overhang above it (Broadway-show-tickets.com), and because the house only holds 1,069 seats, AVFMS reviewer in Rear Mezz L row G called it 'excellent vantage without feeling far removed'.

Lena Horne's boxes sit tight to the proscenium of this narrow 1,069-seat Nederlander house, and both NYTix and TickPick explicitly warn the angle is 'extremely skewed' / 'more side-on' — private but not viable for shows with choreography or full-stage staging like SIX.
